Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

open.name: The astrolabe
missingEvidence: Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Origin disputed: stereographic projection is attributed to Hipparchus (2nd century BCE) and treated by Ptolemy (Planisphaerium); the oldest surviving treatise is by John Philoponus (about 550 CE), the first astrolabes in the Islamic world are credited to al-Fazari (8th century), and the earliest surviving instrument is dated 927–928 CE. Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

missingEvidence: Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays (1088): magnetised needle and magnetic declination; Zhu Yu, Pingzhou Ketan (written about 1111–1117): use at sea; Alexander Neckam in Europe (about 1187–1190). Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

open.name: Mechanical clock with verge-and-foliot escapement
missingEvidence: Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: Anonymous, probably in northern Italy or England, late 13th century: the earliest tower clocks are recorded from about 1283–1300 (Dunstable, Westminster, Canterbury) and the first clear drawing of an escapement is in the Dondi manuscript (1364); the Salisbury Cathedral clock (about 1386) is an early surviving example whose original escapement is uncertain. Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

open.name: The mainspring and fusee
missingEvidence: Full original/archaeological evidence for the following retained claim: The spring-driven clock appears in the early 15th century; the oldest surviving fusee clock is a table clock made for Philip the Good of Burgundy, dated by its decoration to about 1430–1435 (a fusee also appears in a crossbow in a manuscript of 1405 and in drawings of Brunelleschi and Leonardo); the common attribution of the fusee to Jacob Zech of Prague (about 1525) is wrong. Broad chronology, priority and any historical measured performance remain unverified; see the report for already-read partial sources.

open.name: The anchor escapement
